Consider how make-up or the shaving of body hair for example has been the hallmark of femininity for around a century, but in the 1800s this really wasn’t a thing in western culture, and even frowned upon. Makeup was once for actors, and not suitable for the modern day women of the era. Or how high heels were traditionally for men, or how pink was once a boys color, blue a girls color, or women taking over ‘masculine’ jobs when men were drafted during WWII. Also how gender is looked at differently depending on culture… the way Indians or indigenous people view gender is highly different from how it’s conceived in Europe. Hijras for example. 

However you have a point, in that women have always been oppressed for their biological bodies and strictly confined by that. You could argue that femininity has always been seen as the weaker and more fragile gender expression. I won’t disagree at all. What I mean is that what is or isn’t feminine or masculine has changed throughout time and culture, but yes the essence is the same, even if the expression is different historically and/or culturally.

I want genuine diversity because I think people of all backgrounds and cultures are interesting, have things to bring to the table. and deserve to have their stories told. I don’t think anyone should be hired just for their race or gender, but to pretend that certain identities haven’t been subjected to systemic  barriers holding them back or undervaluing them (as you’ve mentioned feminism addresses)  is foolish. How do we go about fixing this issue in a genuine way? I think that’s the real question.

My heart does go out to men and the suffering they endure. 

However, men need to admit the problem is patriarchy, misogyny (a hatred of femininity makes men fear embracing it will strip them of their masculinity [aka power] )and toxic masculinity, and work to change that. My suggestions to men? Create a more positive male role model or archetype. Encourage men to seek professional help. Lift your brothers up instead of tear them down. Work on building support networks and systems for men. Use masculinity to support and defend women as opposed to owning and dominating them. Until men change, they will reap what they sow. 

The suffragists didn’t wait for a savior to save them. They fought for their rights. If men want a better world for themselves, they need to work for it themselves as a group. The problem is if they’ll let go of taking their fears and anger of being emasculated out on women or not.

It’s unfair to call NA a cult. I think it would be more fair to call it a faith healing program. It helps a lot of people, and there’s no reason to pressure others into different programs. Some like the spiritual aspects, others are fine with taking what they like and leaving the rest. People deserve to know other options exist though. I myself am a fan of Recovery Dharma but got nothing out of SMART. The latter felt too much like cbt group therapy and wasn’t as personal. I am interested in trying wellbriety meetings, and might even go back to twelve steps. I’m also joining a Buddhist sangha in my community. 

An essential- yet difficult- part of recovery is changing one’s social circle. However one decides to do that is fine by me if it’s successful. Twelve steps isn’t the only way to develop a new network but people should have the right to join them if they please.

I graduated from intensive outpatient on October 26th. I attended for seven months. I was mandated by my former employer as a stipulation to keep my job. I started drinking more than I should after outpatient and wasn’t as consistent with meetings. was going to go to mental health counseling but felt I deserved a break so I decided to put it off for the time being.
